docs.text: gtracr gtracr simulates cosmic ray trajectories through Earth's geomagnetic field and computes geomagnetic rigidity cutoffs (GMRC). It back-traces particle paths by integrating the relativistic Lorentz force equation in Cartesian coordinates, using the IGRF-14 magnetic field model. Three integration solvers are available (RK4, Boris, RK45), and a tabulated IGRF lookup table provides ~7x speedup over direct spherical harmonic evaluation. Installation Requirements Python >= 3.10 C++14 compiler (GCC, Clang, or MSVC) meson >= 1.1, ninja numpy, scipy, tqdm From source git clone https://github.com/kwat0308/gtracr.git cd gtracr git submodule update --init pip install -e . --no-build-isolation Quickstart import gtracr print(gtracr.__version__) # e.g. "2.0.0" Single trajectory from gtracr.trajectory import Trajectory traj = Trajectory( zenith_angle=45., azimuth_angle=0., rigidity=20., location_name="Kamioka", bfield_type="igrf", ) data = traj.get_trajectory(get_data=True) print(traj.particle_escaped) # True = allowed trajectory Geomagnetic cutoff map from gtracr.geomagnetic_cutoffs import GMRC gmrc = GMRC(location="Kamioka", iter_num=10000, bfield_type="table", solver="rk45") gmrc.evaluate_batch(dt=1e-5, max_time=1.) az, zen, cutoffs = gmrc.bin_results() See the detailed guides for single trajectories and cutoff maps .

docs.text: Magnetic Field Models gtracr exposes three Python magnetic field classes via gtracr.bfield . All three share the same interface and can be used directly — for example, to query the field at a point or to drive the pure-Python fallback integrator. from gtracr.bfield import MagneticField, IGRF14, IGRFTable Classes MagneticField — ideal dipole Evaluates the first-order term of the geomagnetic scalar potential (1/r³ falloff). Fastest to evaluate; useful for coarse studies or sanity checks. Uses the IGRF-14 g10 coefficient at 2025.0 (29 350.0 nT). from gtracr.bfield import MagneticField bf = MagneticField() Br, Btheta, Bphi = bf.values(r=6.371e6, theta=1.0, phi=0.0) IGRF14 — spherical harmonic model Full IGRF-14 evaluation up to degree 13 using time-interpolated Schmidt quasi-normalized coefficients (valid 1900–2030). from gtracr.bfield import IGRF14 from gtracr.utils import ymd_to_dec bf = IGRF14(curr_year=float(ymd_to_dec("2024-01-01"))) Br, Btheta, Bphi = bf.values(r=6.371e6, theta=1.0, phi=0.5) Parameter Description curr_year Decimal year for coefficient interpolation (e.g. 2024.5 ). nmax Truncation degree (default: 13, the maximum in IGRF-14). IGRFTable — pre-computed lookup table Trilinear interpolation over a pre-computed 3D grid (64 × 128 × 256 in r, θ, φ). ~7x faster than IGRF14 for repeated queries. Covers 1–10 Earth radii; the dipole approximation is used outside this range. The table is generated automatically on first use and cached to gtracr/data/igrf_table_<year>.npy and igrf_table_<year>_params.npz . Subsequent runs load the cache directly. from gtracr.bfield import IGRFTable bf = IGRFTable() # builds or loads cached table for today's date Br, Btheta, Bphi = bf.values(r=6.371e6, theta=1.0, phi=0.5) Parameter Description igrf_obj Optional pre-built C++ IGRF object. Built from igrf14.json if None . verbose Print progress while generating the table (default False ). Common interface All three classes implement: bf.values(r, theta, phi) -> numpy.ndarray shape (3,) Returns (Br, Btheta, Bphi) in Tesla at geocentric spherical coordinates (r [m], theta [rad], phi [rad]) . Clearing the table cache If you need to regenerate the cached lookup table (e.g. after updating the IGRF coefficients or changing the evaluation date), delete the relevant files from the data directory: rm gtracr/data/igrf_table_*.npy gtracr/data/igrf_table_*_params.npz The table will be regenerated on the next run.

docs.text: Conventions Arrival direction zenith_angle and azimuth_angle give the arrival direction : the point on the sky the particle comes from, seen from the detector. Zenith: 0 = from overhead, 90 = horizontal, > 90 = up-going (the particle crossed the Earth). Azimuth: measured from geographic north, clockwise seen from above: 0 = from north, 90 = from east, 180 = from south, 270 = from west . This is the astropy AltAz convention and the one of MCEq's location-centred atmospheres. In the local tangent frame x = east, y = north, z = up the unit vector toward the source is (sin z sin a, sin z cos a, cos z) . For positive particles the east–west effect makes cutoffs from the east (azimuth 90) higher than from the west (270). Converting from other conventions Source Its azimuth b gtracr azimuth gtracr < 3.0 0 = from south, 90 = from east (Honda) (180 - b) % 360 Honda / HKKM flux tables 0 = from south, 90 = from east (180 - b) % 360 CORSIKA PHI momentum azimuth, counter-clockwise from magnetic north (x = N, y = W) (180 - b) % 360 , then add the magnetic declination for geographic north East (90) and west (270) are the same in all of these; north and south swap. Units and constants Rigidity R in GV, R = p c / (|Z| e); momentum p in GeV/c; energy is the total energy in GeV. SI conversions use the exact SI values: e = 1.602176634e-19 C, c = 299792458 m/s, 1 GeV/c = 1e9 e / c kg m/s, 1 GeV/c^2 = 1e9 e / c^2 kg. Earth radius 6371.2 km (the IGRF reference radius); altitudes are above this sphere.

docs.text: Geomagnetic Cutoff Rigidities The GMRC class computes geomagnetic rigidity cutoffs — the minimum rigidity a cosmic ray must have to reach Earth from a given direction at a given location. Cutoffs are determined via Monte Carlo: random (zenith, azimuth) directions are sampled, and for each direction the code scans rigidities from low to high until the trajectory escapes Earth's field. Angles give the arrival direction; azimuth 0 = from north, 90 = from east, clockwise (see Conventions ). Two evaluation modes evaluate() — Python-orchestrated Supports all field types ( "igrf" , "dipole" , "table" ). Uses ProcessPoolExecutor for igrf / dipole and ThreadPoolExecutor for table (GIL released in C++). from gtracr.geomagnetic_cutoffs import GMRC gmrc = GMRC(location="Kamioka", iter_num=10000, bfield_type="igrf", solver="rk4", n_workers=8) gmrc.evaluate(dt=1e-5, max_time=1.) evaluate_batch() — C++ batch mode (fastest) The entire MC loop — RNG, coordinate transforms, rigidity scanning, and threading — runs in a single C++ call via BatchGMRC . Requires bfield_type="table" . Achieves ~35k trajectories/second with solver="rk45" . gmrc = GMRC(location="Kamioka", iter_num=10000, bfield_type="table", solver="rk45") gmrc.evaluate_batch(dt=1e-5, max_time=1., base_seed=42) Pass base_seed for reproducible results. If omitted, a random seed is chosen at runtime. Cutoffs outside the scanned range For bisection, every sampled direction is kept. rcutoff is clipped to the scanned rigidity range [min_rigidity, max_rigidity] (both ends included): rcutoff == min_rigidity : the lowest rigidity already escapes, the cutoff is at or below min_rigidity ; data_dict["above_rmax"] is True : no scanned rigidity escapes, the cutoff is above max_rigidity and rcutoff holds max_rigidity as a lower bound. Mask these directions or raise max_rigidity if the high cutoffs matter. Getting results bin_results() (recommended) Bins MC samples into a regular (azimuth, zenith) grid. Fast and appropriate for large sample counts. az_centres, zen_centres, cutoff_grid = gmrc.bin_results( nbins_azimuth=72, nbins_zenith=36 ) # cutoff_grid shape: (36, 72), NaN where no samples fell interpolate_results() (legacy) Scattered interpolation via scipy.interpolate.griddata . az_grid, zen_grid, cutoff_grid = gmrc.interpolate_results() Parameters location also accepts a gtracr.location.Location object with explicit latitude, longitude and altitude (km). This is useful when a downstream atmosphere model supplies the site geometry. Its coordinates take precedence over the built-in location table, even if its name matches a registered site. The same object is accepted by Trajectory(location_name=...) . GMRC constructor Parameter Default Description location "Kamioka" Predefined detector location. iter_num 10000 Number of MC samples. bfield_type "igrf" Field model: "igrf" , "dipole" , or "table" . particle_type "p+" Particle label. date today IGRF date ( "yyyy-mm-dd" ). min_rigidity 5. ( 0.3 for penumbra) Lower bound of rigidity scan (GV). max_rigidity 55. ( 100. for penumbra) Upper bound of rigidity scan (GV). delta_rigidity 1. Rigidity step size (GV). n_workers physical CPUs Number of parallel workers. solver "rk4" Integrator: "rk4" , "boris" , or "rk45" . atol 0. Absolute tolerance (RK45, dimensionless). rtol 1e-7 Relative tolerance (RK45). escape_factor , time_factor 4 , 80 Escape criterion (see below); 0, 0 = fixed 10 R_E / max_time . method "bisection" "bisection" or "penumbra" (see below). ladder_delta 0.005 Penumbra: relative rung spacing. coarse , guard 8 , 2 Penumbra: adaptive-scan parameters. store_ladder False Penumbra: keep the allowed/forbidden flag of every rung. evaluate_batch() parameters Parameter Default Description dt 1e-5 Time step in seconds. max_time 1. Integration time per trajectory (seconds); lower bound of the rigidity-aware budget. base_seed None Integer RNG seed for reproducibility. Random if None . zenith , azimuth None Penumbra only: explicit directions (degrees) instead of iter_num random draws. Penumbra-resolving cutoffs ( method="penumbra" ) The default method="bisection" assumes that every rigidity above the cutoff is allowed and every rigidity below it is forbidden. It returns the first escaping rigidity that the bisection lands on. Inside the penumbra, where allowed and forbidden bands alternate, that value is none of the standard cutoffs. Directions above max_rigidity are retained and flagged. method="penumbra" scans a geometric rigidity ladder R_k = R_min (1 + δ)^k, k = 0 … K−1, K = ⌈ln(R_max/R_min)/ln(1+δ)⌉ + 1. Rung k covers [R_k/√q, R_k √q] with q = 1 + δ. For every direction, evaluate_batch() returns the cutoffs of Cooke et al. (1991): key definition r_upper (R_U) upper edge of the highest forbidden rung r_lower (R_L) lower edge of the lowest allowed rung r_eff (R_eff) R_U − Σ allowed rung widths in [R_L, R_U] (= bottom ladder edge + Σ forbidden widths); also stored as rcutoff flag 0 resolved; 1 nothing forbidden (cutoff below the ladder, R_L = R_U = R_eff = bottom edge); 2 top rung forbidden (R_U, R_eff are lower bounds) Every direction is kept, including flag 1 and 2. R_eff is the cutoff to use for fluxes: a sharp cut at R_eff gives the same transmitted rigidity range as the band structure, measured in linear rigidity. The top rung centre may lie slightly above max_rigidity . gmrc = GMRC(location="Kamioka", bfield_type="table", solver="rk45", method="penumbra", min_rigidity=0.3, max_rigidity=100., ladder_delta=0.005) # fixed grid of directions zen, az = np.meshgrid(np.arange(0., 181., 5.), np.arange(0., 360., 5.)) gmrc.evaluate_batch(zenith=zen.ravel(), azimuth=az.ravel()) r_eff = gmrc.data_dict["r_eff"] Adaptive scan. First every coarse -th rung is traced, plus the bottom rung. Each coarse interval within guard intervals of an allowed/forbidden change is then traced rung by rung. The other intervals take the common value of their two end rungs. With coarse=1 every rung is traced and the result is exact on the ladder. The adaptive scan can miss a band narrower than one coarse interval if it lies away from every detected change, most often an isolated allowed band low in the penumbra. When that happens R_L moves a lot, but R_eff hardly changes. Two IGRF directions at Kamioka (δ = 0.5 %, 0.3–100 GV) each missed a single allowed rung: R_L moved by 22 % and 12 %, R_eff by 0.4 %. In a 0.3–100 GV global study with the same scheme, adaptive and full-ladder R_eff agreed to 0.41 % rms. R_eff changed by 0.35 % rms between δ = 0.5 % and 0.25 %. Use R_L only from full-ladder scans. Transmission functions. With store_ladder=True , gmrc.ladder holds the rung centres and gmrc.ladder_allowed (shape (n, K), bool) the allowed/forbidden flag of every rung and direction. Averaging the flags over directions gives a transmission function. When to use. Use penumbra mode whenever the cutoff feeds a flux calculation, a cutoff map at low or mid latitudes, or any direction close to the horizon. These are the cases where the penumbra is wide. Bisection is fine for quick looks where an error of a few GV inside the penumbra does not matter. Escape criterion A back-traced trajectory is allowed when it reaches the escape radius before it returns below the starting altitude, and forbidden when it returns or runs out of time. gtracr scales both limits with the rigidity of each trajectory (all solvers, the single-trajectory path and both GMRC modes): r_esc = max(escape_radius, k · C_St(p)), t_max = max(max_time, N · r_esc / (β c)), where C_St = R_E √(B0 R_E |q| / p) is the Störmer length and B0 = √(g10² + g11² + h11²) the dipole strength of the active field model, computed once per tracer. Trajectory , GMRC and TrajectoryTracer.set_escape_scaling accept both parameters. Why. The fixed 10 R_E / 1 s criterion counts slowly escaping trajectories as forbidden: below about 10 GV, where 4 C_St exceeds 10 R_E, it overestimates the cutoff (dipole R_L at 60° up to 18 % high; South Pole 0.20 instead of 0.067 GV). Against N = 640 the defaults give R_eff within 0.5 % (dipole, Oulu) and 3 % at the South Pole (quasi-trapped orbits). Validity. Only the internal field is modelled; beyond the magnetopause (about 10 R_E on the day side) the real field is not IGRF. Cutoffs below about 1 GV, at high latitudes, remain model values in either criterion; an external field model (e.g. Tsyganenko) lowers them further. Cost. Unchanged above about 10 GV. Bisection at mid latitudes costs ×1.1–1.4; full high-latitude penumbra ladders ×7–17. A forbidden trajectory at 0.3 GV runs about 3·10⁷ RK4 steps of 10 µs (r_esc ≈ 56 R_E); the step budget is capped at 2·10⁸. docs.text: The GMRC class computes geomagnetic rigidity cutoffs — the minimum rigidity a cosmic ray must have to reach Earth from a given direction at a given location. Cutoffs are determined via Monte Carlo: random (zenith, azimuth) directions are sampled, and for each direction the code scans rigidities from low to high until the trajectory escapes Earth's field. Angles give the arrival direction; azimuth 0 = from north, 90 = from east, clockwise (see Conventions ).

docs.text: Supports all field types ( "igrf" , "dipole" , "table" ). Uses ProcessPoolExecutor for igrf / dipole and ThreadPoolExecutor for table (GIL released in C++). from gtracr.geomagnetic_cutoffs import GMRC gmrc = GMRC(location="Kamioka", iter_num=10000, bfield_type="igrf", solver="rk4", n_workers=8) gmrc.evaluate(dt=1e-5, max_time=1.)

docs.text: The entire MC loop — RNG, coordinate transforms, rigidity scanning, and threading — runs in a single C++ call via BatchGMRC . Requires bfield_type="table" . docs.text: The default method="bisection" assumes that every rigidity above the cutoff is allowed and every rigidity below it is forbidden. It returns the first escaping rigidity that the bisection lands on. Inside the penumbra, where allowed and forbidden bands alternate, that value is none of the standard cutoffs. Directions above max_rigidity are retained and flagged. method="penumbra" scans a geometric rigidity ladder R_k = R_min (1 + δ)^k, k = 0 … K−1, K = ⌈ln(R_max/R_min)/ln(1+δ)⌉ + 1. Rung k covers [R_k/√q, R_k √q] with q = 1 + δ. For every direction, evaluate_batch() returns the cutoffs of Cooke et al. (1991): key definition r_upper (R_U) upper edge of the highest forbidden rung r_lower (R_L) lower edge of the lowest allowed rung r_eff (R_eff) R_U − Σ allowed rung widths in [R_L, R_U] (= bottom ladder edge + Σ forbidden widths); also stored as rcutoff flag 0 resolved; 1 nothing forbidden (cutoff below the ladder, R_L = R_U = R_eff = bottom edge); 2 top rung forbidden (R_U, R_eff are lower bounds) Every direction is kept, including flag 1 and 2. R_eff is the cutoff to use for fluxes: a sharp cut at R_eff gives the same transmitted rigidity range as the band structure, measured in linear rigidity. The top rung centre may lie slightly above max_rigidity . gmrc = GMRC(location="Kamioka", bfield_type="table", solver="rk45", method="penumbra", min_rigidity=0.3, max_rigidity=100., ladder_delta=0.005) # fixed grid of directions zen, az = np.meshgrid(np.arange(0., 181., 5.), np.arange(0., 360., 5.)) gmrc.evaluate_batch(zenith=zen.ravel(), azimuth=az.ravel()) r_eff = gmrc.data_dict["r_eff"] Adaptive scan. First every coarse -th rung is traced, plus the bottom rung. Each coarse interval within guard intervals of an allowed/forbidden change is then traced rung by rung. The other intervals take the common value of their two end rungs. With coarse=1 every rung is traced and the result is exact on the ladder. The adaptive scan can miss a band narrower than one coarse interval if it lies away from every detected change, most often an isolated allowed band low in the penumbra. docs.text: Muon Transport (mutracr) MuonTracer — nicknamed mutracr — transports batches of atmospheric muons between production and decay: RK4 integration of the Lorentz force with continuous dE/dX energy loss, accumulated multiple-scattering (Fermi–Eyges) variance, and deposition of the expected decay weight at each step midpoint (decays are never sampled). Units MuonTracer uses the atmospheric-muon literature convention — not the SI units of Trajectory : quantity unit position cm (Earth-centred Cartesian, z = geographic north) momentum / energy GeV magnetic field Tesla density g/cm³ dE/dX GeV/(g/cm²) time s Quickstart import numpy as np from gtracr import MuonTracer mt = MuonTracer(bfield="shell", atmosphere="usstd", r_ground=6.3712e8) # one 3 GeV/c muon, 20 km above the pole, going straight down x = np.array([[0.0, 0.0, mt.r_ground + 2.0e6]]) p = np.array([[0.0, 0.0, -3.0]]) res = mt.trace(x, p, q=[-1], deposit=dict(kind="bank")) print(res["fate"][0]) # 1 = reached ground (see mutracr.FATES) print(res["deposited"]) # expected decays along the path print(res["bank"]["e_mu"][:3]) # decay deposit rows Configuration Constructor arguments: bfield — "none" , "dipole" (gtracr's ideal centred dipole), "shell" (IGRF-14 tabulated on an (h, colat, lon) grid over the atmospheric shell, trilinear interpolation, built once at construction; validated against direct IGRF to <0.1%), or ("uniform", (bx, by, bz)) in Tesla. atmosphere — "none" , "usstd" (Linsley/CORSIKA US-Std analytic layers), ("uniform", rho0) , or ("table", h_cm, rho) for sampled profiles (e.g. MSIS); evenly-spaced tables get a direct-index fast path. dedx — constant stopping power or (e_kin_grid, a) table (interpolated linearly in ln E_kin, clamped), e.g. from MCEq's continuous-loss table. r_ground — ground-sphere radius in cm. Default 6371.2 km (gtracr's Earth radius); MCEq-matched work uses 6391 km. Tracing and deposit consumers trace(x, p, q, pol=None, w=None, ...) marches all rays to termination ( ground / stopped / faded / escaped / maxsteps ) with per-ray adaptive time steps ( ctl_bend , ctl_loss , ctl_decay , ctl_path control the per-step bend angle, fractional energy loss, decay probability and path length). A step crossing the ground is cut back to the chord crossing (interpolated linearly in r), so grazing rays end within ~10 cm below the sphere. The returned dict contains the final states, per-fate weights, and a weight_audit (deposited + residual weights ≈ total source weight). Decay deposits are consumed by one of three built-in accumulators (selected with the deposit= argument): dict(kind="bank", w_thresh=0.0) — raw deposit rows (position, direction, energy, charge, polarization, MCS sigma, weight) for downstream composition, e.g. with the Michel kernels below. The MCS sigma is the value before the step's own increment. dict(kind="spectrum", e_edges=...) — per-charge E_mu histograms of Σw and Σw·pol. Memory-light; use for large batches. dict(kind="angular", e_edges=..., d_edges=..., axis=(0,0,1)) — per-charge (E_mu, angle-to-axis) histograms of Σw, Σw·pol, Σw·σ²_MCS plus an overflow tally. Rays are independent, so trace parallelises over n_threads std::thread workers (default: all cores) with the GIL released. Per-ray results are bit-identical for any thread count. Michel kernels gtracr.mutracr also provides the polarized μ → ν decay kernels used to turn decay deposits into neutrino fluxes: rest_kernel(x, cos_th_s, pol, kind) — rest-frame dN/(dx dΩ), kind in ("numu", "nue") . lab_spectrum(e_nu, e_mu, pol, kind, charge) — angle-integrated lab spectrum per decay (normalised to 1). lab_kernel(e_nu, cos_th_lab, e_mu, pol, kind, charge) — lab-frame double-differential kernel toward a detector direction. The polarization sign convention is pinned against the MCEq decay database helicity polynomials. Performance About 780 000 rays/s on 32 cores (dipole field, spectrum tally; python examples/eval_mutracr_benchmark.py --full ); the bank consumer is allocation-bound, so prefer the tallies for large runs. Backward characteristics and source integrals MuonTracer.trace_backward(x, p, q, ...) traces from an observation state toward possible production points. Momentum is always the physical forward momentum ; do not reverse the input momentum or charge. Backward propagation reverses spatial drift and magnetic curvature, increases energy under inverse continuous losses, and decreases the probability of surviving to observation. The upper absorbing sphere is r_ground + h_escape ; set h_escape=1.128e7 for a 112.8 km atmosphere. Forward trace is unchanged. With backward arc length s [cm], physical unit direction u, total energy E, stopping power a(E), density rho and momentum magnitude p, the equations are dx/ds = -u du/ds = -(KP / C_CMS) q (u x B) / p dE/ds = rho a(E) dA/ds = m_mu / (p C_CMS tau_mu) survival = exp(-A) The phase-space focusing of the differential intensity is J = a(E_past)/a(E_obs) for these separable losses (J = 1 when a = 0); it is not a derivative of endpoint energies between neighbouring curved rays. The returned arrays are x, p, survival, jacobian, path, steps_per_ray, fate . e_max is a total energy limit [GeV]; path_max is cm (None means no path cap). survival_min , max_steps and positive ctl_bend, ctl_loss, ctl_decay, ctl_path bound the work. Final steps are clipped at the ground, TOA, energy and survival limits. BACKWARD_FATES maps codes to maxsteps, ground, e_max, faded, toa, path_max . By default bank=True also returns midpoint quadrature rows with x, phat, e_mu, q, ray, ds, survival, jacobian, w , where w=survival*jacobian*ds . A source integral is the sum of w*q_source for each ray. Source values must be per cm; include density if a cascade source is per g/cm². Bank rows preserve ray/path order across thread counts. This source quadrature has finite numerical error; refine the step controls to establish convergence. For a fused compiled source without path storage, pass bank=False and source=dict(h_cm=..., cos_theta=..., e_mu=..., values=...) . Axes must be strictly increasing, with at least two finite nodes each; e_mu is total energy above the muon mass. Values have shape (2,nH,nMu,nE,nCol) , with charge order (+1,-1). cos_theta is the local zenith cosine of the arrival direction , -phat·r̂ (positive for downgoing muons, as in MCEq), so a grid on [0, 1] covers all downgoing directions. Interpolation is linear in altitude, cosine and ln(total energy); the source vanishes outside the grid. Signed response columns are supported. The output source_integral has shape (N,nCol). The C++ BackwardSourceConsumer interface supports more general source evaluators; consumers may run concurrently on distinct ray indices. See examples/mutracr_backward.py for a nominal plus signed source example. Backward transport follows deterministic characteristics only: no adjoint angular diffusion for multiple scattering and no spin precession. Ground geometry is spherical and the density profile radial.

Interpolation is linear in altitude, cosine and ln(total energy); the source vanishes outside the grid. Signed response columns are supported. The output source_integral has shape (N,nCol). The C++ BackwardSourceConsumer interface supports more general source evaluators; consumers may run concurrently on distinct ray indices. See examples/mutracr_backward.py for a nominal plus signed source example. Backward transport follows deterministic characteristics only: no adjoint angular diffusion for multiple scattering and no spin precession. Ground geometry is spherical and the density profile radial.

docs.text: Solvers gtracr provides three integration methods for the relativistic Lorentz force equation, all implemented in C++. Comparison Solver solver= B-field evals/step Step size Key properties Frozen-field RK4 "rk4" 1 Fixed Default; O(h^4) with frozen-field O(h^2) error Boris pusher "boris" 1 Fixed Symplectic; ~30% faster than RK4; 2x better momentum conservation Adaptive RK45 "rk45" ~6 (FSAL) Adaptive Dormand-Prince; uses atol / rtol ; ~100x fewer steps for escaping trajectories When to use each solver Single trajectory visualization Use "rk4" or "boris" with bfield_type="igrf" : Fixed time steps produce regularly spaced output points, good for plotting. All three solvers advance the state in Cartesian (ECEF) coordinates, which are regular at the geographic poles, and report the spherical six-vector. RK4 is the safe default. GMRC cutoff scanning Use "rk45" with bfield_type="table" : Adaptive stepping takes far fewer steps for escaping trajectories. Combined with the tabulated IGRF (~7x faster field evaluation), this gives the highest throughput (~35k trajectories/s in batch mode). Default tolerances ( atol=0 , rtol=1e-7 ) resolve cutoffs to the 0.5 % ladder rung (see below). High-precision work Tighten the RK45 tolerance: traj = Trajectory(..., solver="rk45", rtol=1e-9) RK45 error norm and tolerances The RK45 step error is measured on the dimensionless state. Position errors are lengths in units of R_E, with tolerance atol + rtol·r/R_E . Momentum errors are in units of |p|, with tolerance atol + rtol . The norm is the RMS over the six components, applied to the error vectors, so it does not depend on the coordinate system. The error is measured on the dimensionless state (position / R_E, momentum / |p_0|), so atol = 1e-3 allows ~6 km in position and 0.1 % in |p| per step. atol rtol Use case 0 1e-6 Coarser tolerance 0 1e-7 Default tolerance 0 1e-10 Reference solutions Benchmarking solvers Run the solver comparison script to compare accuracy and performance: python examples/eval_solver_comparison.py --n-perf 100

docs.text: Single Trajectories The Trajectory class evaluates a single cosmic ray trajectory through Earth's geomagnetic field. Basic usage from gtracr.trajectory import Trajectory traj = Trajectory( zenith_angle=45., azimuth_angle=0., rigidity=20., location_name="Kamioka", ) data = traj.get_trajectory(get_data=True) The returned dictionary contains time and the six-vector in spherical coordinates: Key Description t Time array (seconds) r Radial distance from Earth's center (m) theta Colatitude (rad) phi Longitude (rad) pr Radial momentum (kg m/s) ptheta Polar momentum (kg m/s) pphi Azimuthal momentum (kg m/s) x , y , z Cartesian coordinates (Earth radii) After evaluation, check traj.particle_escaped to determine if the trajectory was allowed ( True ) or forbidden ( False ). Parameters Required (one of energy or rigidity) Parameter Type Description zenith_angle float Angle from local zenith (degrees). 0 = overhead, 90 = horizontal. azimuth_angle float Azimuth of the arrival direction from geographic north, clockwise (degrees): 0 = from north, 90 = from east. See Conventions . energy float Total energy in GeV (mutually exclusive with rigidity ). rigidity float Rigidity in GV (mutually exclusive with energy ). Optional Parameter Default Description location_name None Predefined location name (overrides lat/lon/alt). latitude 0. Geographic latitude (degrees). longitude 0. Geographic longitude (degrees). detector_altitude 0. Detector altitude above sea level (km). particle_altitude 100. Atmosphere interaction altitude (km). plabel "p+" Particle type: "p+" , "p-" , "e+" , "e-" . bfield_type "igrf" Field model: "igrf" , "dipole" , or "table" . date today IGRF evaluation date ( "yyyy-mm-dd" ). solver "rk4" Integrator: "rk4" , "boris" , or "rk45" . atol 0. Absolute tolerance (RK45 only, dimensionless; see Solvers ). rtol 1e-7 Relative tolerance (RK45 only). escape_altitude 10 * RE Minimum escape radius in meters. escape_factor , time_factor 4 , 80 Rigidity-aware escape criterion (see Geomagnetic cutoffs ); 0, 0 = fixed escape_altitude / max_time . Integration parameters ( get_trajectory ) Parameter Default Description dt 1e-5 Time step in seconds. max_time 1. Integration time in seconds; a lower bound of the rigidity-aware budget unless time_factor=0 . get_data False Return trajectory data dictionary. use_python False Use the pure-Python fallback integrator instead of the C++ extension. Useful for debugging; slower. Solver choice For single trajectory visualization , use solver="rk4" or solver="boris" with bfield_type="igrf" . These fixed-step solvers produce regularly spaced output, which is better for plotting. Boris is ~30% faster than RK4 with 2x better momentum conservation. RK45 uses adaptive stepping (variable output spacing) and is best suited for fast cutoff scanning in GMRC evaluation . See the Solvers guide for a detailed comparison. Predefined locations Kamioka, IceCube, SNOLAB, UofA, CTA-North, CTA-South, ORCA, ANTARES, Baikal-GVD, TA. Example from gtracr.trajectory import Trajectory # 20 GV proton from the east at Kamioka, using Boris pusher traj = Trajectory( zenith_angle=45., azimuth_angle=90., rigidity=20., location_name="Kamioka", solver="boris", ) data = traj.get_trajectory(get_data=True) if traj.particle_escaped: print("Allowed trajectory") print(f" Final radius: {data['r'][-1]:.0f} m") print(f" Steps: {len(data['t'])}")
